cues.text: Let us now turn to some additional reasoning about security configuration, starting with the site-to-site VPN.
When you build a site-to-site VPN, you are joining two separate networks across an untrusted path, so there is a checklist of things you must define.
First, you define the peers, meaning the two gateway devices that will terminate the tunnel.
Second, you define the local and remote subnets, and these must be non-overlapping.
If both sites used the same address range, a router could not tell which side a destination belongs to.
Third, you configure IKE authentication, which is how the two peers prove their identity to each other during the key exchange, together with compatible cryptographic proposals.
Compatible is the key word here: both ends must offer at least one matching set of algorithms, otherwise negotiation fails.
Fourth, you define the IPsec child security associations.
These are the actual protected channels, set up under the IKE negotiation, that carry your data traffic.
Fifth, you define traffic selectors or routes, which say precisely which traffic is sent into the tunnel.
Sixth, you configure firewall rules, and seventh, NAT exemptions where needed, so that traffic destined for the tunnel is not translated before it is encrypted.
Configuring is not enough, so you verify.
Check that the security associations are established.
Check the byte counters, which show whether traffic is really passing through the tunnel.
Check that the traffic is actually protected.
And test recovery, meaning that the tunnel comes back properly after a failure or interruption.
Next, an access control example.
In an authorised lab, a Huawei advanced ACL can express a subnet restriction.
An ACL is an access control list, an ordered set of rules that permit or deny traffic.
The example reads as follows.
The first line is: acl number 3000.
This creates an advanced ACL, identified by the number 3000.
The second line, indented, is: rule 5 permit tcp source 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 destination 192.168.30.10 0 destination-port eq 443.
Let us read it piece by piece.
Rule 5 is the rule number, which sets its order of evaluation.
It permits TCP traffic.
The source is 192.168.20.0 with the wildcard mask 0.0.0.255, which means any host in the 192.168.20.0 slash 24 network.
The destination is the single host 192.168.30.10, and the wildcard of 0 means all bits must match exactly, so it is exactly that one host.
Finally, destination-port eq 443 means the destination port equals 443, which is the port used by HTTPS.
So this rule allows that source subnet to reach one server over HTTPS.
The third line is: rule 10 deny ip source 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 destination 192.168.30.0 0.0.0.255.
Rule 10 denies all IP traffic from the same source subnet, 192.168.20.0 with wildcard 0.0.0.255, to the whole destination network 192.168.30.0 with wildcard 0.0.0.255.
Because rule 5 comes first, the permitted HTTPS flow to 192.168.30.10 is allowed, and everything else from the 192.168.20 network into the 192.168.30 network is denied.
This is shown as configuration text only; we are explaining it, not claiming it has been run.
Now, writing the ACL does nothing until it is applied.
Apply it in the correct interface and direction, and set an explicit policy for the remaining traffic, meaning whatever matches neither rule.
Unmatched behaviour and syntax depend on the platform and feature, so never assume.
Then verify both allowed and denied traffic, proving that what should work works and what should be blocked is blocked.
And take care to avoid locking out management, otherwise you may cut off your own access to the device.
Finally, some points on non-repudiation and secure transfer.
Non-repudiation is the ability to provide evidence that a party performed an action.
It is supported by signatures, trustworthy identity, protected audit records, and timestamps.
But it is not an absolute guarantee; it is evidence, not magic.
Also remember that SFTP and SCP use SSH, unlike plaintext FTP, which sends its data without encryption.
And consider the case of bank branches linked through IPsec.
Here you should demonstrate tunnel protection, plus segmentation, and application-level authorisation.
In other words, the encrypted tunnel is only one layer; you must also separate networks and make sure applications themselves check who is allowed to do what.
